newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia may let Nizhnevartovsk oil firm pay debts.
newsitem.headline: Russia may let Nizhnevartovsk oil firm pay debts.

text.p: Russia may allow oil company AO Nizhnevartovskneftegaz, against which it has initiated bankruptcy proceedings, six weeks to pay off debts to the federal budget, a spokeswoman for Privatisation Minister Alfred Kokh said on Tuesday.
"If it (Nizhnevartovskneftegaz) pays its debts, then why bankrupt it?" said Viktoriya Vergelskaya.
"However, since the decision to initiate bankruptcy proceedings was taken by the (federal) commission on current issues, then obviously the commission will have the last word."

Viktor Pali, the company's general director, told a press conference on Tuesday he had held talks with Kokh, and agreed that Nizhnevartovskneftegaz would raise credits of $200 million over the next six weeks in order to pay of its budget arrears.
"Kokh said that if I find the credit, then he will have nothing against Nizhnevartovskneftegaz, or me personally," Pali said.
But Vergelskaya said Kokh would not take the ultimate decision on the issue, and had made no commitments.
Pali also said the Czech Investment Industrial Fund group, which owns around five percent of shares in the company, was willing to supply the credit.
No comment was immediately available from the fund.
AO Nizhnevartovskneftegaz owed the federal budget 1.10 trillion roubles ($190 million) as of June 1.
Nizhnevartovskneftegaz is the main production unit of the Tyumen Oil Company, which produced 21.30 million tonnes of crude oil in 1996, down six percent from 1995 levels.
There are plans to sell 40 percent of the Tyumen Oil Company in an investment tender and a further 48.68 percent of shares in a special government auction.
Moscow is struggling to rein in huge debts to the federal budget among Russia's energy sector.
